name: Thread & Co.
blurb: A mid-priced apparel brand with 900 stores. Everything is made at 40 supplier factories in Karvan and two other countries, and the largest Karvan factory employs 2,000 people. Founder Elodie Marchetti holds 26% of the vote.

directors.name: Dominic Aldrich
directors.title: Attorney
directors.motive: You know that if a Thread supplier collapses and Thread knew of the risk, a court will care about what the board was told. You want a record that shows the board considered the question, whichever option wins, because your name goes on the minutes. The pension fund that wrote to the company has also asked for your reading of the agreement.

directors.name: Nasrin Haque
directors.title: Labor director
directors.motive: You speak for the workers in the factories that make Thread's clothes, and you have seen the exits, including the ones that were chained shut. You support the binding agreement, though you know that if factories close, your members lose the jobs the agreement is meant to make safe, and many of them are your neighbors. You will be asked by your members how you voted, and you intend to tell them.

directors.name: Teodor Brandt
directors.title: Fund partner
directors.motive: Your fund owns 8% and holds the stock for a quarterly return. You think a $12 million commitment is affordable, and you also think competitors who skip it will undercut Thread on price. You sit on another board that signed something similar and lost a retailer, and you were the one who proposed it.

directors.name: Camille Roux
directors.title: Founder's friend
directors.home: Elodie Marchetti, the founder (first design partner)
directors.motive: Elodie Marchetti has told you she wants to sign, then told you she is afraid of the lawsuits. She holds 26% of the vote, and she has asked you to find out what the others think without saying what she thinks. You designed the first collection with her in a rented garage, and you do not want to see the company hurt or to see her hurt in public.

directors.name: Rahel Tesfaye
directors.title: Community seat
directors.motive: You represent Karvan's exporters, and your members depend on Thread's orders. You want safe factories and you also want the orders to keep coming, and the largest factory owner is your cousin by marriage. You know that if Thread walks away, another brand will pay less attention to the exits. The minister who is your friend has told you to be careful what you say.

briefing.intro: It is January 2013 and a special meeting of the Thread & Co. board has been called. Thread is a mid-priced apparel brand with 900 stores, started by Elodie Marchetti and her first design partner. Everything it sells is made at 40 supplier factories in Karvan and two other countries, none of them owned by Thread, and the largest Karvan factory employs 2,000 people. Directors are paid partly in company stock. Thread is publicly traded, and most of its profit comes from a low cost per garment that Karvan makes possible. A coalition of labor groups has asked every large buyer for an answer by 15 February.
facts: In November a fire at a Karvan garment factory killed 112 workers, who were trapped behind locked and blocked exits. Thread did not buy from that factory, but two of its competitors did, and photographs of burned labels have appeared in the press. A reporter from a national paper has asked Thread to list its Karvan suppliers by Friday and has not said what the paper will do with the list.

Since then a coalition of labor groups and a few European brands has circulated a proposed binding safety agreement. Brands that sign would pay for independent inspections of every factory they use, publish the reports, share the cost of repairs, and stop ordering from any factory that refuses to fix serious hazards. The agreement runs five years and workers' unions could enforce it in court. The coalition says the legal text is still being drafted and the terms may change.

Only two companies, both European, have signed. The coalition says it will announce the agreement once enough large buyers join, and it hears that a third brand will sign next month if one more large buyer does. Several large buyers in North America have said they will not accept binding terms that expose them to lawsuits, and have offered their own voluntary safety programs instead.

Thread already pays for social audits at all 40 suppliers. The audits are done by a private firm on an announced schedule and check wages, hours and exits. They do not examine the structure of the building, and the firm has said that structural checks would need a different contract. Locked exits were the cause of the November deaths, and Thread's audits would have been expected to catch them.

Thread's own sourcing staff estimate that a proper structural inspection of its Karvan factories would find that between 10% and 30% of them need major repairs. They cannot say more because no engineer has been inside most of them. Many of the buildings are older than the garment trade and some have floors added on top. An engineer's report would take three months and about $400,000 to commission.

The owner of Thread's largest Karvan factory is a cousin of a government minister. He has told Thread's sourcing head that an inspection will find nothing and that he will move to a rival buyer if Thread forces repairs. Sourcing believes the factory has added a floor, though no one at Thread has seen the plans.

The binding agreement is projected to cost Thread about $12 million over five years in inspections and repair contributions, against annual earnings of $210 million. Karvan factories have said that if buyers force repairs, some owners will close rather than pay, and about 3,000 workers per closed factory could lose their jobs.

Karvan is a poor country, and garments are 80% of its exports. The government has said it welcomes better safety but warns that buyers who walk away would hurt the workers they say they want to protect, and it will not pay for repairs. The trade association says other countries are waiting to take Karvan's orders.

Customers in Thread's home market have started to ask where their clothes are made. A survey Thread commissioned says 60% of customers say they care and 9% say they would pay more. Thread's largest department-store customer has asked in writing whether Thread's factories are inspected, and Thread's mid-priced rivals are cutting prices.

A voluntary program offered by other buyers would cost Thread about $3 million a year, run by the buyers themselves, with no union role and no legal duty to pay for repairs. Labor groups call it a way to appear active without taking on liability, and its first public report would not appear for a year. Thread's closest competitor has said it will wait to see what the trade association proposes.

Thread's stock is at $22, with 90 million shares outstanding, and the stock moves little on safety news. Investors have not yet asked about Karvan, though one pension fund that holds 3% has sent a letter asking how Thread monitors building safety.

Thread's legal staff say that a binding commitment creates a duty that a voluntary program does not, that a voluntary program does not protect a company that knew of hazards and did not act, and that a court would treat an unread inspection report as knowledge. Thread's insurer covers losses abroad only if the company followed reasonable safety practice, and no one can say what a court would call reasonable, though it offers a small premium discount to companies that commission structural inspections.

decision.lead: Thread's senior management team has been asked to attend the meeting. The Board Chair, who is also the CEO, plans to open by proposing four alternatives. The board must select one by the end of the meeting:

options.title: Sign the binding agreement
options.text: Commit to independent inspections, public reports, shared repair costs and a rule against ordering from factories that refuse to fix serious hazards.

options.title: Join the buyers' voluntary program
options.text: Pay into the program run by other brands, commit to inspections without a legal duty to fund repairs, and publish a summary report each year.

options.title: Strengthen our own audits
options.text: Add structural inspections to Thread's existing audit contract, share the results with suppliers privately, and decide on repairs factory by factory.

options.title: Reduce exposure
options.text: Move orders away from the riskiest Karvan factories to other countries over twelve months, and sign nothing until the new supplier base is in place.

reveal.case: Rana Plaza and the Bangladesh Accord, 2012-2013
reveal.text: The real case is the Bangladesh garment industry. A fire at the Tazreen Fashions factory on 24 November 2012 killed 112 workers. PVH and Tchibo had already signed earlier agreements with labor groups, and the Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh was drafted in the months that followed, with the text dated 13 May 2013. Few large buyers signed before the Rana Plaza building collapsed on 24 April 2013, killing 1,134 garment workers a day after cracks appeared. Signatures then rose quickly, and more than 200 brands and retailers had signed by late 2013. Walmart and Gap declined, citing liability concerns, and on 10 July 2013 17 North American retailers formed the Alliance for Bangladesh Worker Safety as a separate, non-binding program that labor groups called weaker than the Accord.

questions: Agency theory describes costs the owner bears when it cannot see what an agent does. Thread cannot see inside its suppliers' buildings. What bonding or monitoring device in the briefing would have reduced that cost, and who would have paid for it?
Thread, as principal, could push risk onto a supplier it does not own. Which option moved risk back onto the brand, and why would owners resist that?
The workers were the people with the most to lose and the least say. What would a board have to do to give them a real voice, and which of your directors was the closest agent for them?
A voluntary program lets a company appear active without taking on a legal duty. When does appearing responsible differ from being responsible, and how can an owner tell?
